validated_work_order.understanding:
`likePatternToRegex` (packages/loot-core/src/shared/likePattern.ts:16) turns every unescaped `%` into `.*` and every unescaped `?` into `.` with no limit, so a user-supplied value compiles into a regex whose `.test()` backtracks catastrophically against real names. The fix belongs where the pattern language is defined so every consumer inherits it, and the refusal direction is the substance of the ticket: the report's money invariant (fixed in PR #9) requires the axis never to be narrower than the query's result set, so a refused pattern must be handled OPENLY.

This version exists to answer the four objections to v4, each re-checked against the source at HEAD (a596d04f) rather than conceded from memory. All four are correct and all four are now fixed.

**Objection 1 — step 4's reference was unreachable.** v4 recorded the reference row count by typing `Food`, but `contains Food` NARROWS the axis: custom-spreadsheet.ts:91-97 wires `categoryLists(narrowCategoriesByConditions(...))`, `canNarrowAxisByConditions` returns true for a single non-OR category condition (budgetDataQuery.ts:98), and `filterCategoriesByConditions` keeps only names matching `%Food%` (budgetDataQuery.ts:249). I ran the real algorithm over the demo budget's 16 categories (mocks/budget.ts:806-834) plus the 2 the setup step adds: `Food` yields 4 rows, not 21. Step 6's "still 21 rows, same total as step 4" was therefore impossible on a correct build. Fixed: the reference is now recorded with NO filter applied (or the value cleared), which is the 21 rows / unfiltered total every later step compares against, and `Food` moved to the negative controls where it belongs.

**Objection 2 — step 11's accepted long value renders the fail-closed signature.** v4 said a 254-character value "narrows to zero rows". It narrows to THREE rows: `categoryLists` appends uncategorizedCategory, offBudgetCategory and transferCategory unconditionally (ReportOptions.ts:395-401), so an accepted value matching no real category still renders those three at 0.00 — byte-for-byte what a fail-closed build renders. Step 11 therefore taught QA that 3 rows is a pass while AC-3 taught them it is the bug. Fixed: step 11 now states the three-synthetic-row outcome, says plainly that this step CANNOT falsify the refusal direction by observation, and points at AC-8's unit test as what pins acceptance at exactly 256 characters. The length refusal itself stays observable in the same step (a 300-character value gives 21 rows), so the step is not vacuous.

**Objection 3 — out_of_scope[6] was false.** v4 claimed the desktop Electron app, sync server and API do not reach `likePatternToRegex`. They do: packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/sqlite/index.electron.ts:158 registers `db.function('UNICODE_LIKE', {deterministic:true}, unicodeLike)` and index.ts:283 registers the same for the non-Electron backend, and unicodeLike.ts:16 calls the helper directly. Deleted and replaced with an accurate enumeration of which backends reach it and what a refusal means on each.

**Objection 4 — the transaction-rules path was an unargued consumer.** v4 counted three consumers; transaction-rules.ts:645-651 compiles a rule's `contains` to `$like` with `'%' + value + '%'` and :657-663 does the same for `doesNotContain` as `$notlike`, both reaching UNICODE_LIKE via aql/compiler.ts:733-743. A rule value with five or more unescaped wildcards, or over 256 characters, will after this change match EVERY transaction under `contains` and NO transaction under `doesNotContain`, silently. Now enumerated as a consumer, the direction is committed to (open, same helper, same reason), and pinned by tests[] cases against transaction-rules.ts's compiled filters rather than left to chance.

**Two errors the review did not catch, found while verifying.** First, spending-spreadsheet.ts:60 is a FOURTH consumer — it calls `filterCategoriesByConditions` directly (not the helper) and feeds the result to `{ category: { $oneof: matchingCategoryIds } }`. On a refused pattern it yields every category id, a superset of what the query returns, which is the safe direction and needs no code change; it is enumerated and given a test case so nobody later "fixes" it into a subset. Second, v4's qa_script step 5 said `%oo` is exactly 4 unescaped wildcards. It is 3: `contains` wraps the value as `'%' + value + '%'`, so `%oo` compiles to `%%oo%`. A 3-wildcard value staying accepted does not prove the cap is 4. The accepted-side boundary is now `%%oo` (pattern `%%%oo%`, exactly 4), which does.

**One unknown from v4 is now resolved on evidence.** v4 asked whether the 256-character cap applies to the raw or the normalised pattern. Both call paths normalise the wrapped pattern BEFORE it reaches the helper — budgetDataQuery.ts:249 passes `getNormalisedString('%' + condition.value + '%')` and aql/compiler.ts:735 passes `getNormalisedString(right)` into UNICODE_LIKE — so the cap is evaluated on the normalised pattern on both sides and the axis and the query cannot disagree about whether a pattern was refused. That is what makes the open direction coherent rather than merely safe.

One honest limitation, carried forward: the demo budget has 16 categories (18 after the QA setup step), so an 8-wildcard pattern over 18 names costs single-digit milliseconds and the multi-minute hang is NOT reproducible in the browser against it. AC-1 is therefore written to what a live browser can actually observe (the axis stays intact and the page stays responsive), and the falsifiable structural form of the timing claim is carried by AC-8's unit test.
validated_work_order.root_cause: `likePatternToRegex` compiles an unbounded number of `%`/`?` wildcards into a single regex source, so the regex engine's backtracking cost grows exponentially with the wildcard count and a user's filter value becomes a denial-of-service vector on the report category axis and on the SQL `$like` path. There is no bound anywhere in the pattern language definition, and because every consumer calls the same helper, none of them has a place to express a limit of its own.
validated_work_order.approach:
Put the bound inside `likePatternToRegex` and make its refusal explicit in the type. Two module-private constants — `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH = 256` and `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS = 4` — are checked before compiling and inside the compile loop respectively. The counter increments only on the unescaped `%` and `?` branches, never on the escaped branch, so `\%` costs 1 and `50\% off` costs 2. Over-long patterns are refused before any regex is constructed. On refusal the function returns `null` instead of a `RegExp`, which pushes the direction question to every call site in the type system rather than leaving it to a default.

The cap of 4 is what the measurement supports, and every wildcard value that existing tests already pin stays inside it: `contains` wraps the value as `'%' + value + '%'`, so `contains '%'` is 3, `contains '?'` is 3, `contains '100\%'` is 2, `contains 'o%'` is 3 and `contains '_'` is 2 — the accepted region changes nothing a user can currently observe. The exact boundary pair for QA is `%%oo` (pattern `%%%oo%`, exactly 4 wildcards, accepted) and `%oo%` (pattern `%%%oo%%`, exactly 5, refused); note that `%oo` alone is only 3 and proves nothing about the cap.

Every consumer then refuses OPENLY, which is the money invariant: on the report axis `contains` keeps a category when `matcher === null || matcher.test(text)` and `doesNotContain` keeps one when `matcher === null ? true : !matcher.test(text)`; on the query side `unicodeLike` returns 1 for a cached `null`, so under `$like` every transaction comes back (equal to the open axis) and under `$notlike` none do (a strict subset of it). Under no operator can the axis end up narrower than what the query returned — which is the defect class fixed in PR #9, and the reason a naive "return no match" refusal would be a money bug rather than a robustness win. `doesNotContain` in particular must return `true` on refusal; negating a match-everything result would drop every category and reintroduce exactly that bug. spending-spreadsheet.ts's direct call to `filterCategoriesByConditions` inherits the same direction for free, because on refusal the filter keeps every category and its `$oneof` is then a superset of the result set.

Three smaller pieces come along because the change makes their comments false or their exports dead. `filterCategoriesByConditions` always reaches `categories.filter(...)` at budgetDataQuery.ts:291 and `Array.prototype.filter` always allocates, so the `list === categories.list` identity shortcut at :151 can never fire once a condition is being evaluated; the comments at :115-125 and :148-150 both promise the input comes back unchanged and are rewritten to say what actually happens (the rebuild at :155-167 runs, holding the same contents in new arrays, and its trailing `.filter(group => group.categories.length > 0)` drops a group that was already empty in the input — no money moves, and `contains '%'` already behaves this way on unmodified main). `canNarrowAxisByConditions` is unexported: it has exactly one caller (:137) and no test imports it, with the reason recorded next to it, satisfying IAC-6's first branch. `REGEX_SPECIAL` loses its `export` for the same reason (zero consumers outside the file), and the `// ? added here` scar is deleted while `// escaped wildcard - treat as literal character` stays.

files.change: Add two module-private constants, `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH = 256` and `MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS = 4`. Change the signature to `export function likePatternToRegex(pattern: string): RegExp | null`. Return `null` when `pattern.length > MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH` before compiling anything. Inside the existing loop, add an `unescapedWildcards` counter incremented only on the unescaped `%` and `?` branches (never on the escaped branch, so `\%` costs 1) and `return null` once it exceeds the cap. Extend the module doc comment with the contract — a `null` means 'this pattern is refused, it was not compiled' — and record why the cap is 4 by pointing at the measured curve (over 300 category names: 3 wildcards 3.1 ms, 4 -> 24.5 ms, 5 -> 181 ms, 6 -> 1045 ms, 7 -> 30 s, 8 -> 171 s, while 200 compiles of the 8-wildcard pattern cost 0.27 ms, so the cost is all in `.test()` and memoisation cannot fix it). Delete `export` from `REGEX_SPECIAL` (no consumers outside this file) and delete the `// ? added here` scar on the escaped-wildcard line, keeping `// escaped wildcard - treat as literal character`.
files.why: This is the single definition of the LIKE pattern language that `UNICODE_LIKE` speaks, so a bound placed here is inherited by every consumer rather than re-implemented at each — which is what IAC-2 asks for. Returning `RegExp | null` instead of a `RegExp` makes the refusal direction a compile-time obligation at each call site instead of a silent default.

files.change: Retype the LRU to `LRUCache<string, RegExp | null>` so a refusal is cacheable. Replace the `if (!cachedRegExp)` presence test with `=== undefined` — `null` is a legitimate cached value and the old falsy test would treat a cached refusal as a miss and recompile once per scanned row, which is the opposite of the point. Return 1 immediately for a cached `null`. On a cache miss, store whatever `likePatternToRegex` returned, `null` included.
files.why: This is the SQL `$like` / `$notlike` path compiled in packages/loot-core/src/server/aql/compiler.ts:733-743, and it is registered as the `UNICODE_LIKE` SQLite function by BOTH backends (index.electron.ts:158 and index.ts:283), so it is reached from the desktop Electron app, the browser app, the API and the sync server. Returning 1 on refusal is what keeps the report axis from becoming narrower than the query's result set: under `$like` every transaction is returned, equal to an axis that kept everything; under `$notlike` none are returned, a strict subset of that axis. It is also what a transaction rule inherits (transaction-rules.ts:645-663), where the same choice means a refused `contains` matches every transaction and a refused `doesNotContain` matches none — the direction is set in one place so it cannot be got wrong per call site.

files.change: In both LIKE branches (`contains` at :246-253 and `doesNotContain` at :258-265), hoist the compiled matcher out of the per-category callback so a refusal is decided once per condition rather than once per category, and handle `null` openly: `contains` keeps a category when `matcher === null || matcher.test(getNormalisedString(textValue))`; `doesNotContain` keeps one when `matcher === null ? true : !matcher.test(getNormalisedString(textValue))`. Drop `export` from `canNarrowAxisByConditions` (its only caller is :137 and no test imports it) and record that reason in its doc comment, satisfying IAC-6's first branch. Rewrite the two comments this change falsifies: the block at :115-125 ('When no condition narrows anything, the input is returned unchanged by identity') and the note at :148-150 ('returns its input untouched whenever it cannot safely narrow') — once a condition is being evaluated, `filterCategoriesByConditions` reaches `categories.filter(...)` at :291, which always allocates, so the identity shortcut at :151 cannot fire; the rebuild at :155-167 runs, holding the same contents in new arrays, and its trailing `.filter(group => group.categories.length > 0)` drops a group that was already empty in the input (no money moves — `contains '%'` already behaves this way on unmodified main).
files.why: This is the report category axis, the money path. Refusing openly is the whole point: a fail-closed axis would hide categories whose transactions the query did fetch, losing their money from every total — the defect class fixed in PR #9. The identity claims in the two comments have to go, because a refusal provably does not return the input by identity. spending-spreadsheet.ts:60 calls `filterCategoriesByConditions` directly and inherits this direction unchanged, so no edit is needed there.

files.change: Frontmatter `category: Bugfixes` and `authors: [Shivam-Fl]`, with a one-line body stating that a wildcard-heavy filter value can no longer hang a report and that a refused pattern now keeps every category rather than dropping them.
files.why: The release-notes CI gate (.github/actions/release-notes/check/action.yml) refuses a merged PR without one, and 'Maintenance' is the wrong category — this changes user-visible behaviour of the report filter.

acceptance.check: In the demo budget with a report filtered on `category contains %%%%%%Z`, the category axis keeps every category and the page stays interactive throughout — no spinner that outlives the settle, and no frozen table that needs a reload. Stated honestly: the demo budget has 16 categories (18 after the qa_script setup step), and an 8-wildcard pattern over 18 names costs single-digit milliseconds, so the multi-minute hang is NOT reproducible there. What the browser can falsify is that a heavy wildcard value is handled at all rather than hanging, and that the axis stays intact; the falsifiable structural form of the timing claim is AC-8.
acceptance.how_to_verify: Follow qa_script steps 1-3, then step 6. The sign of failure is not slowness alone: the row count collapses from the 21-row reference recorded in step 4 to the three synthetic rows.

acceptance.check: The bound lives inside `likePatternToRegex` and nowhere else: `packages/loot-core/src/shared/likePattern.ts` contains the wildcard-counting and length logic, and neither unicodeLike.ts nor budgetDataQuery.ts contains any — both only handle a `null` the helper returned.
acceptance.how_to_verify: `grep -rn 'MAX_UNESCAPED_WILDCARDS\|MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH' packages/` returns hits in likePattern.ts and its test only. Read the diff of unicodeLike.ts and budgetDataQuery.ts and confirm each adds `null` handling (an `=== null` test, a `matcher === null` branch) and no counting.

acceptance.check: A refused pattern keeps the axis OPEN. `categoryLists` unconditionally appends Uncategorized, Off budget and Transfers (ReportOptions.ts:395-401), so the observable failure signal is NOT an empty table — the guards at grouped-spreadsheet.ts:56 and custom-spreadsheet.ts:108 are unreachable for this input shape. It is that the category list COLLAPSES TO THOSE THREE SYNTHETIC ROWS. With the 18-category QA budget and Split:Category: a correct build renders 21 rows (18 + 3 synthetic); a fail-closed build renders 3. With Split:Group: correct renders 4 rows (3 groups + Uncategorized & Off budget); a fail-closed build renders 1.
acceptance.how_to_verify: qa_script steps 4 and 7: record the reference row count with NO filter applied (21 for Split:Category), then enter `%%%%%%Z`. The axis must still show 21 rows and the same total. Three rows means fail-closed. QA does NOT untick 'Show uncategorized' or 'Show off budget' to look for an empty table — those toggles filter transaction data, not axis rows (`filterHiddenItems` is applied to query data inside `recalculate`, while rows are built by mapping over `groupByList` at custom-spreadsheet.ts:298), so they would not produce that signal.

acceptance.check: Ordinary values filter exactly as today, and so do the escaped-wildcard values. `\%` narrows to exactly `50% off` and `_` narrows to exactly `C_Sharp` ONLY in a budget where the qa_script setup step has created those two categories. In the un-augmented demo budget both narrow to the three synthetic rows — no category name there contains a literal `%` or `_` — and that is the CORRECT result there, not a failure; it is only indistinguishable from fail-closed if asserted without the setup step, which is exactly what the previous plan did.
acceptance.how_to_verify: qa_script steps 2-3 create `50% off` and `C_Sharp`; step 4 records the 21-row reference with no filter applied. Then `contains oo` keeps only Food; `contains \%` keeps only `50% off`; `contains _` keeps only `C_Sharp`; `contains 50\% off` keeps only `50% off`; `contains Food` keeps only Food. A wildcard `_` would have kept all 18 — one survivor is what proves it is literal. Each of those narrows to 4 rows (the survivor plus the three synthetic rows), which is distinct from the 21-row reference and from the 3-row failure signal.

acceptance.check: The bound is the measured one: a pattern of more than 4 unescaped `%`/`?` wildcards, or longer than 256 characters, is refused, and a pattern of exactly 4 is accepted. acceptance.check: The query side is paired with the axis: `unicodeLike` returns 1 for a refused pattern, so under `$like` every transaction is returned (equal to an axis that kept everything) and under `$notlike` none are (a strict subset of that axis). The cached null is not recompiled per row, which is what the `=== undefined` sentinel exists for.

qa_script: Start the app (`yarn start`), open it, and choose 'Don't use a server' then 'View demo' on the initial setup screen. Use the demo budget, NOT 'Start budgeting' — a prior plan's inventory of 7 categories came from default-db.sqlite, while 'View demo' runs createTestBudget (mocks/budget.ts:746, via WelcomeScreen.tsx:130), which creates 16 categories in 3 groups. Open Reports > Custom report.

SETUP — create two categories, so the escaped-wildcard steps below have something to narrow to. Go to the Budget page and hover any category group in the left sidebar; click the 'Add category' button (aria-label 'Add category') and type `50% off`, which saves as you type; press Escape. Do the same and type `C_Sharp`. This leaves 18 categories. Skip this step only to confirm the negative case: without it, `\%` and `_` correctly narrow to the three synthetic rows, which is why a previous plan's assertion could not distinguish that from the bug.

In the Custom report sidebar turn ON 'Show empty rows' (ReportSidebar.tsx:493). It is required for every count below — `filterEmptyRows` returns `!showEmpty ? showHide : true` (filterEmptyRows.ts:24), so with it off, zero rows are hidden and the axis cannot be observed. Leave Split on its default 'Category'. Do NOT untick 'Show uncategorized' or 'Show off budget' to look for an empty table: those toggle transaction data, not axis rows.

REFERENCE — record the baseline with NO filter applied: do not add a filter row yet (a filter row with its value cleared is equivalent). Record the exact row list and count, and the total. With the 18-category budget and Split:Category this is 21 rows — the 18 categories plus Uncategorized, Off budget and Transfers, which `categoryLists` appends unconditionally at ReportOptions.ts:395-401. Record the total too. Every later step is compared against this. Do NOT use an ordinary value such as `Food` for the reference: `contains Food` NARROWS the axis to Food alone and yields 4 rows, which is not the reference.

ACCEPTED SIDE, ordinary — add a filter row (field `Category`, condition `contains`) and type `oo`. This is 2 unescaped wildcards and must be accepted. The axis narrows to Food alone plus the three synthetic rows: 4 rows, total for Food only.

ACCEPTED BOUNDARY — replace the value with `%%oo`. As a `contains` value this compiles to the pattern `%%%oo%`, which is exactly 4 unescaped wildcards, and must be accepted. 4 rows (Food plus the three synthetic). If the axis stays at 21, the cap is not 4. Note that `%%oo` and not `%oo` is the value that tests this: `%oo` compiles to `%%oo%`, only 3 wildcards, so its being accepted proves nothing about the cap.

REFUSED BOUNDARY — replace the value with `%oo%`. This compiles to `%%%oo%%`, exactly 5 unescaped wildcards, and must be refused. The axis keeps EVERY category: 21 rows, the same total as step 4. Three rows here means fail-closed.

HEAVY WILDCARD — replace the value with `%%%%%%Z` (8 wildcards). Same expectation: 21 rows, unchanged total, page responsive the whole time. If the row count collapses to 3 (Uncategorized / Off budget / Transfers, all 0.00), the refusal direction is wrong. Switch Split to Group and repeat: correct is 4 rows (3 groups plus Uncategorized & Off budget); a collapse to 1 means fail-closed.

OPERATOR MIRROR — change the condition to `does not contain`, leaving the value at `%%%%%%Z`. The axis must again keep all 21 rows. This is the direction that reintroduces the money bug if it is implemented as a negated match-everything: the symptom is a collapse to 3 rows, with the report totals reading 0.00 while transactions clearly exist.

ESCAPED WILDCARDS — back to `contains`. `\%` must narrow to exactly `50% off` plus the three synthetic rows (4 rows). `_` must narrow to exactly `C_Sharp` plus three (4 rows) — one survivor proves `_` is a literal and not a SQL wildcard, since a real SQL `_` would have kept all 18. `50\% off` narrows to exactly `50% off`. `?` narrows to all 21, because `?` is this language's single-char wildcard. `%` narrows to all 21.
NEGATIVE CONTROLS — `oo` keeps only Food (4 rows). `Food` keeps only Food (4 rows). These confirm ordinary values are untouched by the bound.

LENGTH BOUND — paste a value of 300 characters. Pattern length 302, refused by length. The axis must show the full 21 rows again, the same total as step 4. Then paste 254 characters: pattern length exactly 256, ACCEPTED, and because no category name contains that run of characters it narrows to the THREE SYNTHETIC ROWS. State this plainly rather than treating it as a pass or a failure: those three rows are byte-for-byte what a fail-closed build renders, so this observation CANNOT falsify the refusal direction. What the pair (300 chars -> 21 rows, 254 chars -> 3 rows) does establish is that the length bound exists and sits between the two. What pins acceptance at exactly 256 characters is AC-8's unit test, not this step.
RELOAD — press F5 with the report still open, and re-enter `%%%%%%Z`. Same 21 rows. This rules out a stale-bundle illusion.

CONSOLE — with the devtools console open, clear it, then step through 8, 9 and 11. No `pageerror` and no unhandled rejection. Console noise from dev-mode (HMR, plugin service) is expected and is not a failure.
risks: The refusal direction is the money invariant. A fail-closed slip in budgetDataQuery.ts or unicodeLike.ts reintroduces the defect class fixed in PR #9, and it is invisible in a small budget because the categories it drops have no money. Mitigated by AC-9 and AC-10 (test) and by the mirror case in custom-spreadsheet.test.ts asserting the totals, not just the row count.

The transaction-rules direction is a silent behaviour change on a path this ticket does not otherwise touch, and the two operators invert: after this change a `contains` rule whose value the bound refuses matches EVERY transaction, and a `doesNotContain` rule whose value is refused matches NO transaction. This is the same open direction the report's money invariant requires, applied consistently, but it is worth naming because a rule that used to apply to a handful of payees would now apply to all of them. AC-11 pins it and the change is bounded by the fact that a value with five or more unescaped wildcards already matched almost everything before it.

The LRU sentinel. Reusing the existing `if (!cachedRegExp)` with a nullable value would treat a cached `null` as a miss and recompile per row — correctness-neutral but a per-row compile cost on exactly the pattern that is already slow to evaluate. AC-10 pins it.

No forbidden path is touched: `.sdlc/memory/**`, `docs/spec/**`, `docs/prd.md`, `docs/trd.md`, `docs/ui.md`, `.github/**` and `.sdlc/**` are all outside files[]. The only non-source file created is a release note under upcoming-release-notes/, which the CI gate requires.
No non-allowlisted host is required: the change is local code and unit tests, and QA runs against `yarn start` on localhost only.

The identity-comments change is a behavioural claim that is easy to get backwards. The new comment must say the lists hold the same CONTENTS but are new arrays and are not returned by identity; stating the opposite would make a correct implementation look wrong to a later reader.
residual_risks: The demo budget is too small to exhibit the original hang, so QA cannot confirm the seconds-to-minutes freeze directly; it can only confirm the axis stays open and the UI stays responsive. The magnitude claim rests on the measured curve (recorded in the likePattern.ts doc comment) plus AC-8's structural test, not on the browser run.

A user on a budget with thousands of categories who currently relies on a 5-wildcard value will see it silently stop filtering — and in a transaction rule, silently start matching every transaction under `contains`. That is the intended trade (5 wildcards is 181 ms at 300 categories and grows from there) but it is a silent behaviour change on both surfaces, which is why the release note says a refused pattern keeps every category rather than dropping them, and why the QA script exercises the accepted side (`%%oo`, exactly 4 wildcards) alongside the refused side.
out_of_scope: Re-measuring or bounding the separate `matches` regex in packages/loot-core/src/server/aql/compiler.ts, which already carries its own `condition.value.length <= 256` guard. The issue body excludes it explicitly.
Routing the Sankey and Budget Analysis graphs through the shared pattern module. Excluded by the issue body; it is issue #84.
Any change to the query-side compiler's regex handling beyond what unicodeLike needs for the nullable return.
Reworking the LIKE pattern language itself — collapsing consecutive wildcards, supporting `_`, or adding escaping for other characters. Those change matching semantics, not cost.
Batching or short-circuiting the category loop in budgetDataQuery.ts (e.g. breaking early once a group cannot match). The bound makes the cost acceptable; the loop is left as it is.
Surfacing a UI message when a filter value is refused. IAC-3 says the axis keeps every category; adding a banner would be a product decision this ticket does not make.

Giving the transaction-rules path its OWN refusal direction. It inherits the helper's, deliberately: one direction, chosen once, is what keeps the axis and the query from disagreeing. A separate rules-only sentinel would be a second decision to keep in sync, and it is not needed for correctness.

alternatives_considered.approach: Memoise the compiled regex (extend the existing LRU in unicodeLike to the report axis too).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It does not address the defect. Measured: 200 compiles of the 8-wildcard pattern cost 0.27 ms while testing it against 300 names costs 171 s, so essentially all of the cost is in `.test()`. The issue body also lists memoisation-whose-only-purpose-is-recompilation as out of scope. (Memoisation is still worth keeping for the refused case, so it is retained — that is a different reason and AC-10 pins it.)

alternatives_considered.approach: Bound the number of wildcards at each call site instead of inside the helper (a cap in budgetDataQuery.ts and another in unicodeLike.ts).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Two implementations that can drift, and the next consumer inherits neither — which is precisely IAC-2's requirement that the bound live inside `likePatternToRegex` so every consumer inherits it. v4's own review established this; it still holds with spending-spreadsheet.ts added as a fourth consumer.

alternatives_considered.approach: Fail CLOSED on a refused pattern: return no match, so the axis drops every category.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It reintroduces the money bug fixed in PR #9. The axis would be narrower than the query's result set, so categories the query fetched would lose their money from every total. Verified against the source: `unicodeLike` returning 1 makes `$like` return everything (equal to the axis) and `$notlike` return nothing (a subset), so the axis is never narrower in either direction. This is also why the failure signal in AC-3 is a collapse to three rows rather than an empty table — the three synthetic rows render regardless.

alternatives_considered.approach: Rewrite the pattern to remove ambiguity (e.g. make consecutive `%` collapse to one `.*`).
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It changes matching semantics rather than bounding cost, and `%%%` already means 'match everything' and is pinned by existing tests in three files. It would still leave a `%` on each side of a long literal run. Out of the ticket's scope.

Length is a necessary guard but not a sufficient one — 8 wildcards in 9 characters is the pathological case that hangs, while a 254-character run of `x` costs nothing. Both bounds are needed, and AC-8 pins both.

It would have been equally defensible on the measurement (3.1 ms vs 24.5 ms across 300 categories), but it changes behaviour for no gain a user can feel, and 4 keeps `contains '%'` and `contains '?'` (both 3) comfortably inside while still excluding the 181 ms tier. The cap is a judgement call and this is the reasoning behind it.

alternatives_considered.approach: Have QA untick 'Show uncategorized' and 'Show off budget' to make an empty table observable, as an earlier review suggested.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Checked against the source and it would not work, so following it would produce a QA script that fails for the wrong reason. `filterHiddenItems` is applied to query data inside `recalculate`, while the rows themselves are built by mapping over `groupByList` (custom-spreadsheet.ts:298), and `categoryLists` appends the three synthetic categories unconditionally (ReportOptions.ts:395-401). Un-ticking those toggles zeroes the synthetic rows' amounts but does not remove them, and with 'Show empty rows' ON they still render. The correct failure signal is a collapse to three rows.

alternatives_considered.approach: Use an ordinary filter value (such as `Food`) to record the QA reference row count, as v4 did.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The action cannot produce the stated result. `contains Food` narrows the axis — `canNarrowAxisByConditions` returns true for a single non-OR category condition and `filterCategoriesByConditions` keeps only `%Food%` matches — so it yields 4 rows, not 21, and v4's own step 10 and budgetDataQuery.test.ts:203 say the same thing. The reference must be recorded with no filter applied.

assumptions: The demo budget is reached via 'Don't use a server' then 'View demo' (WelcomeScreen.tsx:130 -> createBudget({testMode:true}) -> createTestBudget), which creates 16 categories in 3 groups; the QA setup step adds 2, for 18.
`add category` in the budget sidebar saves as the user types, so no explicit Save click is needed.
The report under test is the Custom report (Reports > Custom report, /custom), reached from the report sidebar's filter control; there is no separate Grouped report route in ReportRouter.tsx.

`getNormalisedString` is applied to the pattern on BOTH sides before it reaches `likePatternToRegex` — budgetDataQuery.ts:249 wraps and normalises, and aql/compiler.ts:735 normalises before emitting UNICODE_LIKE — so the length and wildcard counts agree between the axis and the query and a pattern cannot be refused on one side only.
unknowns: Whether normalising before counting can change a pattern's length across the 256 boundary: `getNormalisedString` maps ß to ss and œ to oe, so a value of 254 ß characters normalises past 256 and is refused. This is the conservative direction and, per the assumption above, both call paths normalise identically, so the axis and the query still agree. It is a note for a maintainer rather than a risk to this change.
Whether any non-English locale normalises a category name to characters that change the wildcard count. No such mapping exists in normalisation.ts today, so this is likewise a maintenance note.
validated_work_order.debate_summary: All four review objections against v4 were re-checked against the source at HEAD rather than conceded from memory, and all four are upheld and fixed in this version. Objection 1 (step 4's reference): upheld — `contains Food` narrows the axis to 4 rows, not the 21 the step claimed, and step 6 contradicted it. The reference is now taken with no filter applied, `Food` moved to the negative controls, and AC-1/AC-3/AC-4 how_to_verify updated. Objection 2 (step 11's 254-character value): upheld — an accepted value matching no category still renders the three synthetic rows, byte-for-byte the fail-closed signature, so the step could not falsify the direction. Step 11 now says so plainly, keeps the observable half (300 chars -> 21 rows), and points at AC-8 as what actually pins acceptance at exactly 256. Objection 3 (out_of_scope[6]): upheld — both sqlite backends register unicodeLike as UNICODE_LIKE, so the desktop app, browser, API and sync server all reach the helper; the entry is replaced with an accurate statement. Objection 4 (the transaction-rules path): upheld — rules reach the same helper through $like/$notlike and v4 left the direction unargued; it is now enumerated, committed to with the open direction and its reason, and pinned by AC-11 and four tests[] cases. Two further errors surfaced during verification and are fixed here: spending-spreadsheet.ts:60 is a fourth consumer of `filterCategoriesByConditions` that v4 did not mention (it inherits the safe superset direction and needs no edit, now covered by a test so it is not later "corrected" into a subset), and v4's accepted-side boundary value `%oo` is 3 wildcards, not 4, so it could not have proven the cap — the boundary is now `%%oo` at exactly 4, paired with `%oo%` at exactly 5. One v4 unknown is resolved: both call paths normalise the wrapped pattern before the helper sees it, so the cap is evaluated consistently on both sides.
validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: Every claim about the source was checked at HEAD (a596d04f), and every number in the QA script was produced by running the real `likePatternToRegex` plus the real wildcard counter over the demo budget's actual category names rather than by hand: the 18-row reference, the 4-row accepted narrowings, the 21-row refusals, the 3-row fail-closed signature, the 4-row Split:Group counts, and the wildcard and length classification of every value in the script. The two prior plans' boundary arithmetic was wrong in exactly the places this version corrects, which is why the numbers here were recomputed independently. What is not verified end-to-end is the timing claim in a live browser against a large budget — the demo budget is too small to exhibit the hang — which is why AC-1 is written to what a browser can observe and AC-8 carries the falsifiable structural form. Confidence is below v4's 91 because the transaction-rules direction is a newly-identified behaviour change on a surface this ticket does not otherwise touch; it is committed with tests and named as a risk rather than deferred, but a reviewer may reasonably want it split into its own ticket.
